title: 684028927561/192NV17: White Lion Inn, Bank Street, Chepstow, NP16 5EL
text:
TRIBIWNLYS PRISIO CYMRU  -  VALUATION TRIBUNAL FOR WALES

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 1 of 7

Appellant: Thomas E Teague agent for Jon Durran (Occupier)

Appellant’s Address: White Lion Inn, Bank Street, Chepstow NP16 5EL

Appeal number: 684028927561/192NV17

The Matter Appealed against: 2017 Rating List

Date of Hearing: Friday 21st September 2018

Appearances: Mr John Keane (agent for the occupier), Mr Greg Overs (for
the respondent Valuation Officer)

Date of Decision: 15th October 2018

Decision of Tribunal: Appeal allowed in part

Members of the Tribunal: Mrs E Price-Suter (Chairperson), Mr T Cook, Mr R
Henley

Tribunal Clerk: Mr G Harris

Introduction

1. This is a summary of the case and is not intended to be an exhaustive
record of the proceedings. However, the parties can be assured that all
the evidence was fully considered by the tribunal when it arrived at its
decision. Consequently, the absence of reference to any statement, or
evidence, should not be construed as being overlooked.

Summary of the Case

2. Mr Keane explained that the matter for consideration by the tribunal
related to a 2017 compiled list appeal in respect of The White Lion Inn,
Chepstow. The appellant contended that the Rateable Value (RV) was too
high at £42,900 and should be reduced to £23,000 with effect from 1st
April 2017.
3. Mr Keane stated that the appeal property was a Grade II listed public
house dating from 1644. It was situated in the centre of Chepstow at the
junction of Bank Street and High Street facing a small square. It was of
traditional stone and brick construction under a multi-pitched tiled roof and
had wooden framed single glazed windows. To the rear was a paved
patio area containing approximately 6 picnic benches.

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 2 of 7
4. The internal trade accommodation comprised a public bar, a rear late
night bar and a coffee shop. Each trade area had a distinct demographic
profile with the public bar being favoured by those in the 35-50 bracket,
the late night bar by 18-25’s and the coffee shop by a more mature
clientele and shoppers.
5. Mr Keane explained that the layout of the pub was quite dispersed with a
central passage effectively separating the coffee shop from the rest of the
property. Consequently, staffing costs were high with an inevitable
element of duplication, these costs had been reflected in the working
expenses of the business. The White Lion had a late licence to serve
alcohol until 1:00am at weekends and could stay open until 1:30. The
premises licence, a copy of which was attached in the appendixes to his
evidence pack, included a mandatory condition to employ door staff
during alcohol sales hours, with the extra costs incurred itemised as a
separate expense in Mr Keane’s valuation.
6. Mr Keane explained that the basis of valuation was set down under
Paragraph 2(1) Schedule 6 of the Local Government Finance Act 1988,
as amended. It was defined as an amount equal to the rent at which it is
estimated the hereditament might reasonably be expected to let from year
to year on the assumptions that -
(a)  the tenancy begins on the day by reference to which the
determination is to be made;
(b)  immediately before the tenancy begins the hereditament is in a state
of reasonable repair, but excluding from this assumption any repairs
which a reasonable landlord would consider uneconomic; and
(c)  the tenant undertakes to pay all usual tenant’s rates and taxes and to
bear the cost of the repairs and insurance and the other expenses (if
any) necessary to maintain the hereditament in a state to command
the rent mentioned above.
For the purposes of this appeal the Antecedent Valuation Date (AVD) was
1st April 2015.
7. Mr Keane stated that the usual methodology for the valuation of public
houses was contained in The Approved Guide to the Valuation of Public
Houses (“the guide”) a copy of which was attached in the appendixes to
his evidence pack. The valuation approach was to estimate the Fair
Maintainable Trade (FMT) of the hereditament, broken down into wet,
food, accommodation and other, and apply a percentage “bid” to each of
those income streams with the resultant figure representing the rateable
value. The Guide divided the country into 3 areas – Central London, Outer
London and Provincial England and Wales and each area into 3 bands –
Category 1 (Upper), Category 2 (Middle) and Category 3 (Lower). There
were 2 bands for food sales – A (Upper) and B (Lower). It was the task of
the valuer to place the hereditament in question into this matrix. In this
case the valuer had placed The White Lion at the bottom of Category 3 for
wet sales and the bottom of Band B for food sales. Mr Keane believed
those choices were constrained by the Guide and contended that the
resulting RV was still too high.

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 3 of 7
8. Referring to Case Law, Mr Keane highlighted the case Sharp v Griffiths
(VO) 1992 where Mr Norman Rose stated that the Guide is, in effect “a
truncated profits method” of valuation that had no statutory basis and was
not binding on individuals or the Valuation Tribunal. In the more recent
Valuation Tribunal for England case Brown v Kirk (VO) the President of
the Tribunal said “the guide is what it says it is, merely a guide, a degree
of subjective decision making is still required of the valuer or on appeal
the Tribunal”. It was Mr Keane’s opinion that the Guide was not flexible
enough to adequately reflect the actual circumstances of The White Lion,
specifically the high wage costs and the expense of employing door staff
and as such a more refined approach was necessary.
9. Mr Keane contended that as the Guide was a “truncated profits method”
that it was appropriate, therefore to use the full profits method to provide a
more nuanced valuation. Mr Keane stated that the profits method was an
established method for the valuation of public houses, although had been
used less frequently since the introduction of the Guide and the insistence
by the Valuation Office on its use.
10. Mr Keane explained the principles behind the profits method and stated
that the starting point was an assessment of the Fair Maintainable Trade
(FMT). Mr Keane had provided the Valuation Officer with detailed Profit
and Loss accounts for the years ending 30th June 2015 and 30th June
2016, copies of which were attached to his appendixes. In this case the
FMT at the AVD had been agreed between the parties as being £408,000
for wet sales and ££42,000 for food sales, being the approximate average
of the 2015 and 2016 trades. For consistency Mr Keane had adopted
approximate averages of the working expenses for his valuation and
commented that the gross profit was in line with market expectations and
as far as he was aware was accepted as reasonable by the Valuation
Officer. Mr Keane’s valuation was as follows –

11. Mr Keane explained that according to the 2016 Cost Guide for Tied
Tenants and Lessees to the Running of a Pub, a copy of which was
attached in the appendixes to his evidence, the average working
expenses expressed as a percentage of turnover for this type of public
house was 33%. The actual working expenses of the White Lion were
43% of turnover, significantly more than the upper end of the range in the
2016 Cost Guide. This disparity was attributable to the exceptional costs
of employing staff and door security. This was reflective of the fact that
the appeal property had 3 distinct trade areas, all of which needed to be
staffed. In addition, door staff had to be employed according to the terms
outlined in the Premises Licence.

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 5 of 7
12. In conclusion, Mr Keane contended that the Approved Guide did not
reflect the exceptional circumstances of The White Lion due to its physical
layout and additional staffing requirements coupled with the legal
requirements to employ door staff which resulted in significantly higher
working expenses than those at the upper end of the licenced trade’s
benchmarking tool. A full profits method valuation provided a more
nuanced valuation which was better able to reflect the individual
advantages and disadvantages of The White Lion. In light of this, Mr
Keane asked that the Tribunal confirm a RV of £23,000.
13. Under cross examination Mr Keane confirmed that he had not departed
from using the Guide in any other valuation of a public house. Mr Keane
explained that the current occupier’s sister had signed the original
tenancy on 1st February 2010 for a period of 15 years with preordained 3
yearly rent reviews. The original rent was for £52,000 per annum, rising to
£60,000 in 2013, £68,000 on the 2nd review, £73,000 on the 3rd and
£83,000 on the 4th. It was Mr Keane’s opinion that the rent was
unsustainable. The current occupier had inherited the lease when his
sister had passed away.
14. Mr Overs, for the Valuation Officer, introduced the appeal property and
provided the Tribunal with external photographs and a plan of its layout.
He explained that it had been entered into the 2017 Rating List at a RV of
£42,900 with effect from 1st April 2017. It had been valued according to
Paragraph 2(1) Schedule 6 of the Local Government Finance Act 1988.
15. Mr Overs explained that public houses, bars and inns were valued on a
rental basis. Traditional public houses use “fair maintainable turnover” as
the comparator to assist in the analysis of rental evidence and therefore
as a valuation basis. Percentage rental bids were then applied to the
various income streams making up the FMT depending on location, age,
modernity, style of operation etc. as set out in the Valuation of Public
Houses Approved Guide.
16. Mr Overs stated that The Pubs Rating Forum had been established in
2014 in order to provide a vehicle through which the pub industry and the
Valuation Office Agency could maintain an on-going dialogue and
exchange of information in respect of matters relevant to the valuation for
rating of public houses. The forum included the following member
organisations –
•
British Beer & Pub Association
•
Association of Licensed Multiple Retailers
•
British Institute of Innkeeping
•
Federation of Licensed Victuallers Associations
•
Guild of Master Victuallers
17. In collaboration with the Forum and its appointed rating advisers (Gerald
Eve, Lawrence Tattersall, BNP Paribas and Davis Coffer Lyons) the
available rental evidence had been analysed and considered in detail,
along with other market performance indicators. The Approved Guide had

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 6 of 7
been agreed with the Forum, following a period of 4 months intensive
discussions covering all relevant factors.
18. Mr Overs explained that the Guide had been used to value all of the
public houses (over 44,000) in England and Wales for the 2017 Rating
List and to his knowledge the VOA had not departed from the Guide in the
defence and settlement of any public house rating appeal.
19. Mr Overs believed that the analysis of the accounts used by Mr Keane in
his valuation showed a healthy income for the property but that the
outgoings appeared exceptionally high giving a low profit margin and
hence a low amount available for rent and rates. Mr Overs contended that
to depart from the Guide in considering the RV of a public house
consideration had also to be made to the actual rent passing on the
property which was stated to be £60,000 with effect from 25th June 2014.
After deducting an amount to represent the domestic element of the
property, the resulting figure would provide a high assessment not
consistent with similar pubs in the locality trading at a similar FMT.
20. Therefore, Mr Overs believed that the only consistent approach to arriving
at the correct RV for the appeal property was to follow the approved
guide. Referring to the Guide, Mr Overs had considered each category
and band and having had regard to the particular disabilities of the
property had adopted the minimum category of both bands for wet and
food trades. In particular he had taken into account the front and rear bars
and the separate shop type premises within the curtilage which required
additional staffing and running costs above the average, and also the
additional door security costs as indicated in the accounts. Mr Over’s
valuation was as follows –

21. In conclusion, Mr Overs urged the tribunal not to depart from using the
Approved Guide in considering the correct RV for The White Lion Inn. In
using the Guide and having regard to the particular disadvantages of the
property, adopting the minimum of the lowest band adequately reflected
the particular hereditament whilst maintaining a consistent approach to
the valuation of public houses. Adopting the minimum of the lowest bands
to the agreed FMT had given a RV of £34,000 with effect from 1st April
2017 which he asked the Tribunal to confirm.

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 7 of 7
22. Under cross examination, Mr Overs believed the rent to be exceptionally
high and not useful as it had been agreed 5 years prior to the AVD
although all evidence was considered depending upon its weight. Mr
Overs agreed that the property was unique but did not believe that this
was enough reason to depart from the Guide, stating that lots of public
houses have more than 2 bars and other pubs in Chepstow employ door
staff.
23. At the conclusion of the hearing, the tribunal decided to reserve its
decision.

The Reasons for Decision

24. Having considered all the evidence placed before it the tribunal decided
as follows: -

25. The Tribunal accepted that there was no dispute between the parties with
regard to the FMT used by each party in their respective valuations. The
dispute centred upon the method of valuation used to obtain the RV of the
hereditament.

26. Mr Keane contended that due to the exceptional circumstances of The
White Lion due to its physical layout and additional staffing requirements,
a full profits method valuation would provide a more nuanced valuation
which was better able to reflect the individual advantages and
disadvantages of hereditament. Mr Overs on the other hand contended
that the property should be valued in accordance with The Approved
Guide to the Valuation of Public Houses.

27. The Tribunal whilst acknowledging that the full profits method could be
used in the valuation of a public house believed that such guidance such
as The Approved Guide, agreed by the VOA and on behalf of a particular
category of ratepayers, in this case The Pubs Rating Forum, ought to be
followed unless there was good reason not to. The Tribunal accepted that
The White Lion Inn had unconventional layout which had resulted in high
staffing costs however did not consider this to be unique in the public
house industry and therefore was not reason enough to depart from The
Approved Guide.

28. The Tribunal was satisfied that Mr Overs had adequately reflected the
characteristics of the appeal property when deciding in which category
and band to place it for his valuation and that his proposed RV of £34,000
was fair and reasonable.  In light of this, the Tribunal orders the Valuation
Officer to amend the RV of The White Lion Inn, Bank Street, Chepstow
NP16 5EL to £34,000 with effect from 1st April 2017.
